title: How to redeem points and miles
summary: A plain-English guide to redeeming points and miles: compare every redemption option, follow a five-step flow, value any award in cents per point, and learn where transfers beat cash by 2 to 5 times.
body_text: The short version Figure out what your trip costs in cash, then pick the redemption that beats that price. That is the whole job. Moving flexible points to airline and hotel partners usually beats cashing them out, often by 2 to 5 times . Judge every redemption in cents per point . Anything over 1.5¢ is good. Over 2.5¢ is great. Transfers are one-way and final . Confirm the seat or room is there before you move a single point. Spending points instead of cash sounds great, and it is. Then you open your account to actually book something and the choices stack up. Transfer partners. Travel portals. Statement credits. Gift cards. Plenty of people freeze right there, leave the points sitting, and never take the trip. This guide is about the other half of the hobby: actually using what you have. We will skip past earning points and go straight to turning a balance into a booked trip. By the end you will know how to get real value out of every point in your account. Points are only worth something the day you use them. The goal was never to hoard. It was to fly. What you can redeem points and miles for Most programs let you spend points a handful of ways, and they are not equal. The same 60,000 points might buy $600 of travel or $3,000 of travel, depending on the method you choose. Here is how the common options compare. Redemption method Typical value Verdict Transfer to airline & hotel partners Premium flights and top hotels 1.5–8¢+ ★ Highest value Book through the card's travel portal Simplicity, wide availability 1.0–1.5¢ Solid & easy Statement credit or cash back Flexibility, no travel needed 0.5–1.0¢ Low value Gift cards, merchandise & shopping Convenience only 0.5–0.8¢ Avoid These ranges are typical outcomes, not promises. What you actually get depends on the route and dates you pick. Redeem your points, step by step Once you have a balance worth spending, the process itself is short. Here is the path from points to booked. 1 Take stock of what you have Write down what you have in each program: credit card points, airline miles, hotel points. Flexible card points from Chase, Amex, Citi, or Capital One matter most here, since they can turn into many different currencies. 2 Decide what the trip is worth Look up the cash price of the flight or hotel you want. That number is your benchmark. It tells you whether a points price is a good deal before you commit to anything. 3 Confirm the award is available Find a specific flight or room with award space before you move any points. This one habit saves more people from regret than anything else. Never transfer on a hunch. 4 Transfer (only if you need to) If your points sit with a card issuer, move them to the partner running that award. Transfers are usually instant and 1:1, but they only go one direction, so there is no taking them back. 5 Book it and pay the taxes Finish the booking in the partner's account. You will usually owe a little in taxes and fees, sometimes a few dollars in place of a few thousand. That is the part that makes the whole thing worth it. Transfer to travel partners, where the value lives If you remember one thing from this guide, make it this: flexible credit card points are worth the most when you transfer them to an airline or hotel program. Chase, American Express, Citi, and Capital One each work with a set of travel brands. Move your points across and you reach award prices the cash-and-portal crowd never sees. Featured transfer partners A few habits keep transfers from going sideways: Confirm award space first. Find the exact flight or room before you transfer a point. Watch for transfer bonuses. Issuers regularly run 20–40% bonuses to certain partners, which is free extra points when your timing lines up. Know the ratio. Most partners transfer 1:1, but a few are worse. Check before you move. Roame tip: Already earning miles directly with an airline or hotel? Skip the transfer step. Book straight from that program's award chart. How much is a point actually worth? There is one number that settles every "is this a good deal?" debate: cents per point (CPP) . It tells you how much value you are squeezing out of each point in a given redemption. CPP = cash price × 100 ÷ points required A $850 flight that costs 50,000 miles gets you 1.7¢ per point. Find that same flight for 25,000 miles and you are at 3.4¢. Higher is better. Run your own trip through the calculator below. Cents-per-point calculator Cash price you’d otherwise pay $ Points or miles it costs pts You’re getting 3.40¢ / point Excellent value This is what award travel is all about. Book it before it is gone. 0¢ 1.5¢ good 2.5¢ great 5¢+ Rule of thumb: if you can't clear about 1.5¢, your points are usually better saved for a redemption that does. High-value sweet spots worth chasing Once you have the basics down, these are the redemptions worth chasing. Each one returns far more value than its point cost suggests. Paris in a lie-flat Flying Blue · from 50,000 miles Air France runs monthly Promo Rewards that knock business class to Europe down to bargain pricing. Tokyo, up front ANA Mileage Club · from 60,000 miles ANA's own first class is one of the better-priced premium awards out there, especially on a round trip. Dubai, on points Hotel points · from 30,000 / night Five-star suites that run $900+ a night routinely open up for a fraction in points. Bali, the long way Qatar Privilege Club · from 70,000 miles Route through Doha in Qsuite, the business class most frequent flyers rank at the top. Frequently Asked Questions What's the difference between points and miles? ⌄ Practically none. "Points" and "miles" are just different names different programs use for the same thing: a rewards currency you can redeem for travel. How much each is worth depends entirely on the program, not the label. What's the most valuable way to redeem? ⌄ Transferring flexible credit card points to airline and hotel partners, then booking premium cabins or high-end stays. That is where you routinely see 2–5¢ per point versus roughly 1¢ for cash back. Should I ever just take the cash back? ⌄ Sometimes, and that is fine. If you have no travel plans coming up or only a small balance, cashing out at about 1¢ beats letting points sit unused. Just know you are usually leaving value behind. Do my points expire? ⌄ Flexible card points generally stay valid as long as your account is open and in good standing. Airline and hotel miles can expire after a stretch of inactivity, though any earning or redeeming usually resets the clock. Transfer to a partner, or book through the portal? ⌄ Transfer when you want the most value and can find award space. Use the portal when the cash fare is already cheap or no good award shows up. Both are fine. It comes down to value versus effort.

title: From A Few Engineers to Real Impact: 10 Years of Brno
summary: When I look back at how we started in Brno, it is hard to believe how far we have come.
body_text: By: Michal Kohoutek, Sr. Director of Engineering, Research & Development When I look back at how we started in Brno, it is hard to believe how far we have come. Interestingly, the story of Brno began with an acquisition that never happened . In 2016, the former NDS business was exploring opportunities to expand its integrated operating room (iOR) capabilities and acquire field programmable gate array (FPGA) expertise to support customizable video processing pipelines for surgical displays and video management systems. During that process, the leadership team discovered a small company in Brno that appeared to be an ideal fit. While the acquisition did not materialize at the time, we uncovered something equally important: the exceptional engineering talent, strong university ecosystem, and innovation potential of the region . That experience left a lasting impression on both the NDS leadership team and our corporate team. Rather than walk away, they recognized an opportunity to build those capabilities organically and made the decision to establish an engineering presence in Brno. Rainer Scholl, Senior Vice President, R&D , was one of the leaders who saw that potential early. We filled several key engineering positions quickly, and the first office space followed soon after. I joined during this formative period after being recruited by Rainer and was inspired by the vision of building a world-class engineering team that could drive innovation and growth for both NDS and our broader organization. What started as a small team of engineers working to establish new capabilities would eventually grow into a strategic location supporting multiple business units and functions across our global organization . Today, as we celebrate ten years in Brno, I am proud of what we have built together and even more excited about what lies ahead. The Early Years The early years were filled with challenges. As Miroslav Dítě, Hardware Team Manager , recalls, we had strong engineering talent and limited clarity on which products to develop and which markets to target. At the same time, Milan Šalomon, Lead System Architect, remembers the transition from a small company environment into a global organization, requiring new processes and ways of working across regions. We also had to prove ourselves. As Jiří Kříž, Sr. Software Design Engineer , recalls, earning trust to take on increasingly complex and business-critical work required persistence and strong execution. Alongside that effort, employees like David Kumhal, Tester and Verification Technician , helped establish the testing and service capabilities that continue to support product quality and reliability today. Even the basics had to be built from the ground up. Petr Kolesnikov, Lead Software Engineer , remembers starting in a simple meeting room while the team developed the infrastructure and tools needed to support future growth. As Marek Vaňura, Product Engineering Manager , recalls, building the site required far more than engineering. Employees stepped in wherever help was needed, establishing processes, sourcing equipment, developing supplier relationships, and creating a workplace where people wanted to stay and grow. Earning Trust Through Results One of the defining milestones was the CD1 project. Both Miroslav and Milan identify it as a turning point. Delivering a complex solution for a major customer with a relatively small team demonstrated what Brno was capable of and helped build confidence with customers and leaders alike. As our capabilities expanded, so did our responsibility. We moved from contributing to individual projects to owning entire product areas and strategic initiatives. What began with FPGA and hardware expertise evolved into full product ownership for iOR (Integrated Operating Room) solutions and expanded support across Advanced Surgery – Insufflators and Pumps, Detection & Analysis, Beam Steering and Scanning Solutions, Light Engines, CO₂ Lasers, product cyber-security, DevOps, automated testing, and other shared engineering services. At the same time, Brno’s impact expanded beyond engineering. Corporate Shared Services established capabilities in accounts payable, accounts receivable, general ledger, master data management, and business systems support, helping create scalable processes and shared expertise that support teams across Europe and North America . Together, these technical and business capabilities strengthened Brno’s role as a strategic contributor across our global organization. Creating Real-World Impact For me, one of the most rewarding aspects of the past ten years is seeing our work reach customers. Many of us came from environments where interesting projects never became real products. Here, we develop solutions that are used every day . That creates a strong sense of purpose and reinforces the importance of staying focused on the customer and the product. Today, Brno supports nearly 200 employees across engineering and business functions and serves as a key contributor across our global organization . Alongside R&D, Corporate Shared Services has evolved from a transactional support function into a center of expertise focused on process improvement, systems support, scalability, and talent development. The team now supports financial operations across multiple regions while helping prepare the organization for future growth through business systems modernization and SAP S/4HANA initiatives. Our teams support the full product lifecycle , from architecture and development through verification, product cyber-security, automation, deployment, and sustaining engineering. Combined with a strong can-do attitude and deep technical expertise , that breadth of capability allows us to solve complex challenges and deliver high-quality solutions. I am especially proud of the role our teams have played in developing advanced iOR products used by healthcare organizations around the world. Whether designing software, testing products, verifying performance, or supporting quality, employees understand that their work can ultimately help healthcare professionals deliver better patient care. Looking Ahead What makes me proudest is not only what we have built, but the people who built it . Many of the employees who helped establish Brno are still here today, continuing to innovate and mentor others , shaping the future of the site. Looking ahead, I see Brno continuing to grow not only as a product development center but also as a competence hub where we can share specialized expertise across teams and business units, creating even greater value for our customers. I also see continued opportunities for Corporate Shared Services to grow as a center of excellence , leveraging Brno’s strong university talent pipeline along with data expertise and our collaborative culture to help scale processes and create additional value for the business. The next ten years will depend on the same principles that brought us this far: staying close to our customers, delivering products that matter, and working together as one team. I am confident our greatest achievements are still ahead of us.

title: Recurring revenue through personalization, data, & scalability
summary: Recurring revenue grows when subscription teams use personalization, subscriber data, and scalable lifecycle experiments to improve retention.
body_text: In 2026, subscriber acquisition costs are at an all-time high for businesses, while switching platforms has become almost frictionless. A subscriber can leave a media platform, retailer, or streaming service in the time it takes to tap "cancel," with a competitor one search away. That imbalance is why retention has become a central part of subscription growth. Annual recurring revenue depends on how well a business keeps the product relevant, responds as subscriber needs change, and creates more reasons to engage between billing cycles. Three areas matter consistently: Personalization built on subscriber behaviour Data that decides which flexible path a subscriber gets when their needs change Scalable ways to extend value beyond the base plan Personalization is retention infrastructure Two subscribers can generate the same number of pageviews and still move in different directions over time. One returns several times a week, reads across categories, and gradually builds a stronger habit. Another consumes a large amount of content in one session, then disappears until the next email arrives. The volume may look similar, but the retention risk is different. In situations like these, generic engagement metrics fall short. Personalization needs to be guided by behaviour, including declining logins, narrowing content categories, reduced feature use, shorter sessions, or fewer meaningful interactions over time. Those signals help teams identify when the subscriber relationship is starting to weaken. DailyMail+ increased 30-day engagement by 14% and lifted customer lifetime value by 32% by using subscriber-level data to shape what each reader saw and when they saw it. The result came from treating content as part of the retention system, with interventions tied to actual subscriber behaviour. Personalization becomes valuable when it changes what happens next for the subscriber. It helps teams decide who needs a new recommendation, who needs value reinforcement, who is ready for an upgrade, and who may need a different intervention before churn risk becomes visible in aggregate reporting. Data for flexibility Cancellation risks cannot be put in one basket. A subscriber may be leaving because of price, lower engagement, temporary circumstances, reduced need, or a weaker sense of value. Each case requires a different response, and the only way to know which one applies is the data behind it: cancellation reason, tenure, engagement history, billing history, and subscriber value. Pause flows, downgrade paths, and plan changes are useful because they create more ways to preserve the relationship before cancellation becomes final. But the options themselves do little without the data to route the right subscriber to the right one. Offered blindly, they become a single generic save screen with extra steps. Without subscriber data behind the decision, flexibility is just a menu of options with no way to know which one to show. A pause flow, for example, should not become a quiet gap before billing resumes. A subscriber who pauses for six weeks and hears nothing may return to a charge they no longer expected or wanted. Data on what that subscriber used the product for before pausing is what turns a silent gap into a relevant mid-pause touchpoint, and a subscriber who receives one returns with more context. The data determines the match. Pausing for a temporary reason may need a path back in. Leaving over price may need a plan change. Disengaging from the product may need value reinforcement before any offer makes sense. Matas increased retention by 29% by using subscriber data to build matched, flexible responses for subscribers at risk of leaving. The result shows why retention teams need data-led paths, rather than one generic save flow applied to every cancellation signal. Scalable growth with extended value The base subscription creates the recurring relationship. Growth improves when teams create more moments for subscribers to engage, discover value, and build habit between billing cycles. A streaming media company grew engagement by 23% and trial signups by 110% by expanding how and when subscribers interacted with the product. A multi-platform media company saw a 7.8% retention lift alongside 163% growth in in-app engagement by creating more reasons to open the app between billing cycles. These results come from widening the surface area of engagement. The subscriber has more moments to experience value, and the business has more signals to understand what is changing. The key takeaway Recurring revenue strengthens when teams use subscriber data to guide personalization, decide which flexible path fits a subscriber when their needs change, and create more reasons to engage across the lifecycle. These areas work together. Behavioural data helps teams identify the right intervention and the right flexible path before cancellation becomes final. Expanded engagement creates more opportunities to reinforce value over time. Subsets helps subscription teams turn this work into a tested system.
